                Sylow intersections and Frobenius ratios

                  Wolfgang Knapp and Peter Schmid


     Abstract. Let G be a finite group and p a prime dividing its order |G|, with
     p-part |G|p , and let Gp denote the set of all p-elements in G. A well known
     theorem of Frobenius tells us that fp (G) = |Gp |/|G|p is an integer. As
     Gp is the union of the Sylow p-subgroups of G, this Frobenius ratio fp (G)
     evidently depends on the number sp (G) = |Sylp (G)| of Sylow p-subgroups
     of G and on Sylow intersections. One knows that sp (G) = 1 + kp and
     fp (G) = 1 + (p − 1) for nonnegative integers k, , and that fp (G) < sp (G)
     unless G has a normal Sylow p-subgroup. In order to get lower bounds
     for fp (G) we, study the permutation character π = πp (G) of G in its
     transitive action on Sylp (G) via conjugation (Sylow character). We will
     get, in particular, that fp (G) ≥ sp (G)/rp (G) where rp (G) denotes the
     number of P -orbits on Sylp (G) for any fixed P ∈ Sylp (G). One can have
      ≥ k ≥ 1 only when P is irredundant for Gp , that is, when P is not
                                                                     
     contained in the union of the Q = P in Sylp (G) and so P = Q=P (P ∩Q)
     a proper subset of P . We prove that  ≥ k when |P | ≤ |P |/p.

     Mathematics Subject Classification. 20D20, 20D35.

     Keywords. Sylow subgroups, Sylow character, Frobenius ratio, p-elements.




1. Introduction. Throughout G will be a ﬁnite group and p a prime dividing
its order |G|. By Sylow, the set Sylp (G) of Sylow p-subgroups of G is nonempty,
and G acts transitively on it via conjugation. Let π = πp (G) denote the asso-
ciated permutation character of G (Sylow character).
    Fix P ∈ Sylp (G). Then |P | = |G|p equals the p-part of |G| and Sylp (G) =
P = {P g : g ∈ G} (where P g = g −1 P g). Each P -orbit on Sylp (G) distinct
  G

from {P } has size a proper power of p. Hence the Sylow p-number sp (G) =
|Sylp (G)| has the form sp (G) = 1 + kp for some integer k ≥ 0. The set Gp =
        g                                                              |P |
  g∈G P of all p-elements in G can be described as Gp = {g ∈ G : g           = 1}.
Hence, by a theorem of Frobenius [2], fp (G) = |Gp |/|P | is an integer, called
10                         W. Knapp and P. Schmid                     Arch. Math.


the Frobenius p-ratio of G. The identity
                                     1  sp (G)
                           fp (G) =
                                    |P |  π(x)
                                          x∈P

is basic for our purposes (see Lemma 3 below). Obviously sp (G) and       fp (G)
remain unchanged when replacing G by G/Op (G) where Op (G) = g∈G P g
is the greatest normal p-subgroup of G. We have P = Op (G) if and only
sp (G) = 1 resp. fp (G) = 1.
    We say that the Sylow p-subgroups of G are irredundant (for Gp ) provided
none can be omitted in order to get Gp as their union. Of course this is true
if and only if the given P ∈ Sylp (G) cannot be omitted. Thus we have irre-
                                               
dundancy in this sense precisely when P = Q∈Sylp (G)\{P } (P ∩ Q) is a proper
subset of P . So P is a T.I. subset of G just when |P| = 1 and, as a rule, fp (G)
is large when |P| is small. We call P strongly irredundant provided |P| ≤ |P |/p.


Theorem 1. Suppose P ∈ Sylp (G) is not normal in G, so that the Sylow num-
ber sp (G) = 1 + kp with k ≥ 1. Then the Frobenius ratio fp (G) = 1 + (p − 1)
                                kp
for some positive integer  < p−1  . We have  ≥ k when P is strongly irre-
dundant, where  > k, unless |P/Op (G)| = p. Conversely, if  ≥ k, then P is
irredundant.

    Thus fp (G) ≥ p (as  ≥ 1). We call k and  the parameters of sp (G)
                                                               kp
and fp (G), respectively. If |G/Op (G)|p = pa , then  ≤ p−1      (1 − p1a ), with
equality precisely when P/Op (G) is a T.I. subset of G/Op (G). Observe that
P is strongly irredundant when P/Op (G) is cyclic or, more generally, when
      
P = x∈P (P ∩ Q)x for some Q ∈ Sylp (G). To see this, use that cyclic p-
groups are uniserial, and that the normal closure of a proper subgroup of a
ﬁnite p-group is a proper subgroup.
    There exist groups G where sp (G) > |Gp |, and then at least one Sylow
p-subgroup of G is redundant for Gp , and we have  < k (see the example in
Sect. 2). One has (1 + k(p − 1))p > (1 + kp)p−1 by binomial expansion. Hence
                p−1
fp (G) > sp (G) p when  ≥ k ≥ 1, and it is conjectured that this inequality
holds in general. Indeed, Gheri [3] has conﬁrmed this in the case where G is
p-solvable, and has reduced this problem to almost simple groups. The authors
have veriﬁed the conjecture for various such groups of small orders. It holds
when G is a group of Lie type of characteristic p; use that then Op (G) = 1
and that fp (G) = |G|p by a celebrated theorem of Steinberg [9].
    Let rp (G) denote the number of P -orbits on Sylp (G), which evidently does
not depend on the chosen P ∈ Sylp (G). If sp (G) = 1 + kp with k ≥ 1, then
2 ≤ rp (G) ≤ 1 + k. We have rp (G) = 2 if and only if P is transitive on the
(nonempty) set Sylp (G)\{P }, which happens when G is a Zassenhaus group of
suitable degree. Also, rp (G) = 1+k if and only if each P -orbit on Sylp (G)\{P }
has size p.
Vol. 123 (2024)      Sylow intersections and Frobenius ratios                   11

                                                                s (G)
Theorem 2. Let sp (G) = 1+kp with k ≥ 1. Then fp (G) > rpp (G) . The Sylow p-
subgroup P of G is strongly irredundant for Gp in the extreme cases rp (G) = 2
and rp (G) = 1 + k.
   In particular, we have strong irredundancy when k ≤ p since then rp (G) = 2
or rp (G) = 1 + k.
Theorem 3. Let sp (G) = 1 + kp with k ≥ 2. Then fp (G) = 1 + (p − 1) with
 ≥ 2, and the Sylow p-subgroup P of G is irredundant for Gp if sp (G) ≤
p(fp (G) + 2).
   Thus fp (G) ≥ 2p − 1 when sp (G) ≥ 1 + 2p, and we certainly have irredun-
dancy when sp (G) ≤ p(2p + 1).
2. The Sylow character. We keep the assumptions and notations as introduced
above. Fix P ∈ Sylp (G). We assume that P is not normal in G so that the
Sylow number sp (G) = 1 + kp with k ≥ 1. Then the Frobenius ratio fp (G) > 1
as well. Recall that the Sylow character π = πp (G) for the prime p is the
permutation character of G in its action on Sylp (G) = P G (counting ﬁxed
points). For x ∈ G, let xG = {xg : g ∈ G} denote the conjugacy class of x in
G (so that |xG | = |G : CG (x)|).
                                                                     r
Lemma 1. Let N = NG (P ) be the normalizer of P in G, and let i=1 N gi P
be the decomposition of G into double cosets mod (N, P ), say with g1 = 1.
Then r = rp (G) is the number of P -orbits on Sylp (G) and sp (G) = |G : N | =
    r
1 + i=2 |P : (P ∩ P gi )|. In fact, the assignments P g → N g for g ∈ G define
an isomorphism from the G-set Sylp (G) onto the G-set G : N = {N g : g ∈ G}
(with G acting via multiplication from the right), and the P -sets P : (P ∩ P gi ),
i > 1, may be identified with the P -orbits on Sylp (G) \ {P }.

Proof. It is well known (and easily veriﬁed) that P G is G-isomorphic to G : N
(see Aufg. 23 on page 32 in Huppert [5]). In particular, π is aﬀorded by the
G-set G : N , and is induced from the 1-character of N . So the remainder is
nothing but Mackey decomposition (see Satz V.16.9 in [5]). The intersections
P ∩ P gi = P ∩ N gi are point stabilizers for the corresponding P -orbits, and
are determined up to P -conjugacy.                                           
    Note that N = NG (P ) is an abnormal subgroup of G [5, VI.11.18]; since
                                            g
NG (N ) = N , one also knows that N g → N   for g ∈ G deﬁnes an isomorphism
from G : N onto N . Of course Ker(π) = g∈G N g , and π(x) ≥ 1 if and only
                      G
        
if x ∈ g∈G N g . Also Op (G) is the kernel of P in its action on Sylp (G), and
Ker(π)/Op (G) is a p -group.
    It is an interesting open question whether sp (G) = |G : NG (P )| can be read
oﬀ from the character table of G (Navarro). Can one then obtain in addition
π as sum of the irreducible characters of G?

Lemma 2. Let x ∈ P and N = NG (P ). We have π(x) = sp (G) · |x|x∩N  G|
                                                                        |
                                                                          and
xG ∩ N = xG ∩ P . Moreover π(x) is the number of Sylow p-subgroups of G
containing x (including P ), and π(x) = 1 + kx p for some nonnegative integer
12                         W. Knapp and P. Schmid                    Arch. Math.


kx ≤ k. If H is a normal subgroup of G, then sp (G) = sp (P H) · sp (G/H) and
π(x) = πp (P H)(x) · πp (G/H)(Hx).
Proof. The ﬁrst statement is well known (see Aufg. 24 on page 32 of [5]). The
p-element x ∈ P normalizes some Sylow p-subgroup Q of G if and only if x ∈ Q
(as Q is a p-subgroup of G of largest possible order, and Qx is a p-subgroup of
G). Moreover xG ∩ N = xG ∩ P . We also have π(x) ≡ 1 (mod p) since each x -
orbit on Sylp (G) has size a power of p, and since |Sylp (G)| = sp (G) = 1 + kp.
The last statement is due to Gheri [3, Lemma 3.6]. Use here that P H/H is a
Sylow p-subgroup of G/H with normalizer N H/H, and consider the partition
of the set of Sylow p-subgroups of G containing x (having cardinality π(x))
where P and Q belong to the same part if P H = QH. Since the Sylow p-
subgroups of G/H are conjugate, there are πp (G/H)(Hx) parts with each
part having cardinality πp (P H)(x).                                            

Of course this again is independent of the chosen particular Sylow p-subgroup
of G. By the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, we have fp (G) ≥ fp∗ (G),
and this inequality is proper since sp (G) > 1, (and π(x) = π(1) for some
x ∈ P ). Clearly sp (G), rp (G), fp (G), and fp∗ (G) remain unchanged when
                                     
replacing G by G/Op (G) (or by Op (G)). Gheri [3] conjectured that always
                p−1
fp∗ (G) ≥ sp (G) p , and conﬁrmed this when G is p-solvable. By Lemma 2, we
know that sp (G) = sp (P H) · sp (G/H) and fp∗ (G) = fp∗ (P H) · fp∗ (G/H) for
any normal subgroup H of G. Arguing by induction on |G|, one thus is readily
reduced to the case where G = P H for some minimal normal subgroup H of
G. Here H will be a p -group when G is p-solvable, whence G p-nilpotent. This
will be treated in Lemma 6 below.

the subset of P consisting just of those x ∈ P for which π(x) > 1; in other
words, π(x) = 1 if and only if x ∈ P \ P.
Proof. This is immediate from Lemma 2.                                          

Proof. We use an idea given in the proof of Proposition 2.1 in [4]. This propo-
sition might be incorrect as it stands, its proof being not conclusive as the

sentence following statement (∗) can only be substantiated when the p-element
considered has order p.
    We have π(x) ≤ π(y) if y ⊆ x . So we may let x have order p. We assert
that there is g ∈ G such that the sets of Sylow p-subgroups of G containing
            i
x and xgx for i = 0, . . . , p − 1 are pairwise disjoint. Then we have 1 + p
such sets, each of cardinality π(x) as π is a class function on G. Hence then
π(x)(1 + p) ≤ sp (G), as desired.
    Assume the assertion is false. Then, for every g ∈ G, there are indices
                                                      i   −i           j−i −1
i = i(g) = j(g) = j such that x, xg = x, xgx x or x, xgx g                  =

xgx , xgx x g are p-subgroups of G. In the latter case, j − i is not divisible

x is subnormal in G, whence x ∈ Op (G) in contrast to our hypothesis.

H. Then sp (G) = |H : CH (P )| and π(x) = |CH (x) : CH (P )| for any x ∈ P .

Example. For odd p the ﬁrst example where a Sylow p-subgroup is redundant
for Gp has been given by Derek Holt, namely for G = PSL3 (7) and p = 3.
This can be found in a post given by Mikko Korhonen in MathematicsStack-
Exchange (2013). There one also ﬁnds the following example by Jack Schmidt
(see also Example 2.5 in [3]):
    Let P be elementary abelian of order pa (a ≥ 2). Let q ≡ 1 (mod p) be
                                                              a
a prime and let H be an elementary abelian q-group of rank pp−1 −1
                                                                   , which is
the number of maximal subgroups Mi of P . There is afaithful action of P
on H such that H/CH (Mi ) has order q for each i (and i CH (Mi ) = 1). The
corresponding semidirect product G = H · P is a p-nilpotent group satisfying
14                             W. Knapp and P. Schmid                  Arch. Math.

                                    pa−1 −1
CH (P ) = 1 and |CH (x)| = q p−1 for any x = 1 in P , because there are
      a−1
just p p−1−1 maximal subgroups of P containing x. Hence sp (G) = |H| and
            pa−1 −1
π(x) = q      p−1     by Lemma 6. We infer that P is redundant for Gp and that
                      p−1                                        a−1       pa −1
fp∗ (G) =  sp (G)    . Moreover |Gp | = 1 + (pa − 1)q p . We have q p−1 >
                       p

       a       pa−1
1 + (p − 1)q        provided q is chosen large enough compared with pa (which
is possible by Dirichlet’s prime number theorem). In this case sp (G) > |Gp |.

3. Proof of Theorem 1. Fix P ∈ Sylp (G), and let Op (G) = 1 (without loss).
Write |P | = pa and sp (G) = 1 + kp (a ≥ 1, k ≥ 1). Let also π = πp (G). Two
nontrivial p-elements x, y of G are said to be related provided x = y . This is
an equivalence relation on Gp = Gp \{1}, each class having cardinality divisible
by p − 1. Thus |Gp | = pa fp (G) − 1 = (pa − 1)fp (G) + (fp (G) − 1) is divisible
by p − 1. Since p − 1 is a divisor of pa − 1, we get that fp (G) − 1 = (p − 1)
for some integer , as required. Clearly  ≥ 1 (as k ≥ 1). From Lemmas 3 and
                                                 kp
2, it follows that fp (G) < sp (G), whence  < p−1   .
          
    Let P = {x ∈ P : π(x) > 1} (Lemma 4). If P is a T.I. subset of G =
                                          
G/Op (G), then |P| = 1 and fp (G) = 1a pa (1 + kp) − kp = 1 + kp(1 − 1a ) =
                                              p                              p
sp (G) − kp
         pa takes its greatest value (in terms of sp (G) and |P |). Here p
                                                                           a−1
                                                                               is a

divisor of k (Frobenius). Let |P | > 1 in what follows, which forces that a ≥ 2.
Using that π(x) < sp (G) for 1 = x ∈ P and π(x) = 1 for x ∈ P \ P from
Lemma 3, we get that
                              1  
                   fp (G) >        |P | + (|P | − |P|)(1 + kp) .

for each x ∈ P by Lemmas 4 and 2, whence by Lemma 3,

Remark. Arguing as above, one gets that |P| = 1 + m(p − 1) for some integer
m ≥ 0 (even |P|/|P|p is of this form). This could be helpful in order to check
whether P is strongly irredundant. Of course there are groups G where a
Sylow p-subgroup is irredundant but not strongly irredundant, and where the
parameters  < k. (For p = 2, such an example is provided by the symmetric
group G = S5 , where s2 (G) = 15 (k = 7) and f2 (G) = 7 ( = 6), and where
π(x) = 1 for any 4-cycle x ∈ G.)

4. Proof of Theorem 2. Without loss let again Op (G) = 1, and let sp (G) =
1 + kp with k ≥ 1. Fix P ∈ Sylp (G) and let π = πp (G) be the Sylow character.
Vol. 123 (2024)      Sylow intersections and Frobenius ratios                   15


    By the Cauchy–Frobenius–Burnside ﬁxed point formula [5, Satz V.13.4]
                                                              1
rp (G) = |P1 | x∈P π(x), which is greater than        x∈P π(x)
                                                               |P |
                                                                    by the
arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. Consequently
                                           sp (G)
                        fp (G) > fp∗ (G) >        ,
                                           rp (G)
as desired. Clearly 2 ≤ rp (G) ≤ 1 + k, and rp (G) = 2 if and only if P is
                                                    
transitive on Sylp (G) \ {P }, in which case P = x∈P (P ∩ Q)x for any Q = P
in Sylp (G).
    Suppose that rp (G) = 1 + k. Then each P -orbit on Sylp (G) diﬀerent from
{P } has size p. It follows that P = P/Op (G) is elementary abelian (as it acts
faithfully on Sylp (G)\{P }). By Brodkey [1] there is Q ∈ Sylp (G) such that
P ∩ Q = 1. But P ∩ Q is a point stabilizer for the P -action on Sylp (G) and
|P : (P ∩ Q)| = p is the size of a P -orbit. Thus |P | = p and, therefore, P is a
T.I. subset of G. It follows that |Gp | = (1 + kp)p − kp and fp (G) = 1 + k(p − 1).
(In general there is no Q ∈ Sylp (G) such that P ∩ Q = Op (G); e.g. see Ito [6].)
Remark. Let D = P ∩ Q be a Sylow intersection of largest order (P = Q ∈
Sylp (G)). Let |P : D| = pb and |NP (D) : D| = pc (1 ≤ c ≤ b). Then the
                                         
contribution to fp (G) resulting from P ∪ x∈NP (D) Qx is just 1 + pc − pc−b ,
because the 1 + pc Sylow subgroups involved intersect pairwise in D. Hence
fp (G) > p except possibly when b = c = 1.
5. Proof of Theorem 3. Let again Op (G) = 1 (without loss), and let sp (G) =
1 + kp with k ≥ 2. Fix also P ∈ Sylp (G), and let |P | = pa . By Theorem 1,
we know that fp (G) = 1 + (p − 1) for some integer  ≥ 1. As usual, we let
π = πp (G).
    We ﬁrst show that the parameter  ≥ 2. Otherwise  = 1 and fp (G) = p,
and we must have a ≥ 2 (since otherwise P is a T.I. subset of G). From
                                 sp (G)
Lemma 5 we get that π(x) ≤ 1+p          for each x = 1 in P . Applying Lemma 3
we obtain that
                          1     pa − 1                      1
            p = fp (G) ≥ a +            (1 + p) = 1 + p − a−1 > p,
                          p        pa                     p
which is the desired contradiction. In particular, fp (G) ≥ 1 + 2(p − 1) = 2p − 1.
    (A diﬀerent approach can be given using the remark following Theorem 2,
which in turn is in the spirit of [7, p. 80].)
    Now let sp (G) ≤ p(fp (G) + 2) or, equivalently, let k < fp (G) + 2. We
assert that then P is irredundant. Assume the assertion is false. It follows
from Theorem 2 that we must have k ≥ 1 + p, for otherwise P were even
strongly irredundant. From Lemmas 4 and 2, we get that π(x) ≥ 1 + p, for
each x ∈ P . Using that π(1) = 1 + kp > 1 + p therefore Lemma 3 shows that
                                 1 + kp         k−1            p
             2p − 1 ≤ fp (G) <            =k−         ≤k−         .
                                  1+p           1+p           1+p
                              p
Consequently k > 2p − 1 + 1+p    , whence k ≥ 2p ≥ p + 2. But this implies that
              k−1
fp (G) < k − 1+p ≤ k − 1 and so k ≥ fp (G) + 2, against our hypothesis.
